questions.q: Which query returns only the name and city columns from the customers table?
options: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name, city
SELECT name, city FROM customers
GET name, city FROM customers
SELECT customers FROM name, city

questions.q: Which condition picks orders shipped to either Pune or Nagpur in one short expression?
options: city = 'Pune' AND city = 'Nagpur'
city BETWEEN 'Pune' AND 'Nagpur'
city LIKE 'Pune, Nagpur'
city IN ('Pune', 'Nagpur')

questions.q: Which function gives the biggest single order amount in the orders table?
options: MAX(amount)
TOP(amount)
COUNT(amount)
HIGH(amount)

questions.q: What does a JOIN do in a query?
options: Adds a new column to a table for good
Copies one table into another table
Combines rows of two tables using a related column
Sorts two tables in the same order

questions.q: Which constraint stops the mobile_no column from being left empty when a row is added?
options: UNIQUE
DEFAULT
NOT NULL
INDEX

questions.q: Your manager wants the number of different customers who ordered in October, counting each customer once. Which expression do you use?
options: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
COUNT(customer_id)
DISTINCT COUNT(*)
SUM(customer_id)

questions.q: orders has 1,000 rows. After a LEFT JOIN from orders to payments the result has 1,150 rows. What is the most likely reason?
options: A LEFT JOIN always adds extra blank rows
Some payments have no matching order
The join removed rows with NULL values
Some orders have more than one payment row

questions.q: Which query lists customers who have never placed an order?
options: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o WHERE o.amount = 0

questions.q: An employees table has a manager_id column. What is a self join used for here?
options: Showing each employee next to their manager's name
Copying the table to another database
Removing duplicate employee rows
Joining two tables without any condition

questions.q: A query LEFT JOINs customers to orders, then adds WHERE o.status = 'paid'. What happens to customers with no orders?
options: They stay, with empty order columns
The query gives a syntax error
They disappear, because their o.status is NULL and fails the WHERE
They appear twice in the result

questions.q: What does a CTE written as WITH monthly AS (...) give you?
options: A permanent new table in the database
A named temporary result the following query can use
An index on the monthly column
A saved login for another user

questions.q: Which ranks salespeople by sales inside each region, starting again at 1 for every region?
options: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY region, sales DESC)
GROUP BY region ORDER BY sales DESC
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY sales)
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sales DESC)

questions.q: Two staff tie for the top sales figure. What do ROW_NUMBER() and RANK() over the same ORDER BY give them?
options: Each function gives them 1 and 2
ROW_NUMBER gives 1 and 2; RANK gives both of them 1
Each function gives them both 1
ROW_NUMBER gives both 1; RANK gives 1 and 2

questions.q: A report on a 2-crore-row orders table filters on order_date and has become very slow. What do you check first?
options: Whether the keywords are in capital letters
Whether adding DISTINCT speeds it up
Whether the table can be split by hand into two
The query plan, and whether order_date has an index it uses

questions.q: WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024 is slow even though order_date has an index. What is the usual fix?
options: Use order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
Put 2024 in quotes as '2024'
Add ORDER BY order_date to the query
Drop the index and create it again

questions.q: Which expression gives a running total of daily sales, day by day?
options: SUM(amount) with GROUP BY sale_date
MAX(amount) OVER ()
SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)
COUNT(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)

questions.q: A wallet app moves ₹500 from one account to another with two UPDATE statements. How do you make sure both happen or neither does?
options: Run each UPDATE in a separate session
Run the second UPDATE before the first
Run them in one transaction and COMMIT only if both work
Add a LIMIT 1 to both UPDATE statements

questions.q: You ran UPDATE products SET price = 0 without a WHERE, inside a transaction you have not committed. What do you do?
options: Run ROLLBACK, then repeat it with the right WHERE
COMMIT, then restore last week's backup
DROP the products table and recreate it
Run another UPDATE setting every price to 100

questions.q: Why put a UNIQUE constraint on the gstin column of a vendors table?
options: So the gstin values sort faster in reports
So the gstin column may be left empty
So the gstin values are stored encrypted
So the database refuses a second vendor with the same GSTIN

questions.q: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 50 GROUP BY city gives an error. Why?
options: GROUP BY must be written before FROM
An aggregate can't be used in WHERE; that condition goes in HAVING
COUNT(*) needs a column name inside it
city must be written inside quotes

questions.q: On the same table, SUM(amount) / COUNT(*) is lower than AVG(amount). What explains this?
options: Some amounts are NULL: AVG skips them but COUNT(*) counts those rows
AVG always rounds the result upward
SUM leaves out negative amounts
COUNT(*) counts only rows with unique amounts

questions.q: You need rows where city is anything other than Mumbai, and rows with no city must be included too. Which condition is right?
options: WHERE city <> 'Mumbai'
WHERE city NOT LIKE NULL
WHERE city <> 'Mumbai' OR city IS NULL
WHERE city != 'Mumbai' AND city = NULL

task.title: Write SQL for a small online shop's sales questions
task.brief: You get two tables from a small online shop (customers and orders) with sample rows. Write one SQL query for each of the three questions in 20 to 25 minutes. Any common SQL dialect is fine; say which one you use. Under each query, add one or two lines explaining how it works and anything you watched out for (cancelled orders, NULL amounts, ties, customers with no orders). Correct logic matters more than exact syntax.
task.material:
Tables (PostgreSQL):

customers(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT, joined_on DATE)
orders(id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(id),
       order_date DATE, amount NUMERIC(10,2), status TEXT)   -- status: 'paid', 'cancelled', 'pending'

Sample rows
customers
id | name          | city      | joined_on
1  | Anjali Rao    | Hyderabad | 2025-02-10
2  | Imran Shaikh  | Pune      | 2025-06-01
3  | Deepa Nair    | Kochi     | 2026-01-15
4  | Harpreet Gill | Pune      | 2026-03-20
5  | Suresh Kumar  | Hyderabad | 2026-08-05

orders
id  | customer_id | order_date | amount  | status
101 | 1           | 2026-10-02 | 1250.00 | paid
102 | 2           | 2026-10-05 | 899.00  | cancelled
103 | 1           | 2026-10-18 | 2400.00 | paid
104 | 4           | 2026-10-21 | 560.00  | paid
105 | 2           | 2026-11-01 | 3100.00 | paid
106 | 5           | 2026-10-30 | NULL    | pending

Questions
Q1. Total paid sales per city for October 2026, highest first.
Q2. Customers (name, city) who have never placed any order.
Q3. For each city, the customer with the highest total paid amount (all time). Show city, name and total.
key_points: Q1 joins orders to customers, keeps status = 'paid' and October 2026 dates, groups by city, sums amount, orders by total DESC
Q1 uses a date range (>= '2026-10-01' and < '2026-11-01') or equivalent, not text matching
Q2 uses LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (not NOT IN with possible NULLs)
Q2 returns Deepa Nair (Kochi) from the sample data
Q3 totals paid amount per customer, then picks the top per city with a window function (RANK/ROW_NUMBER over PARTITION BY city) or a correlated subquery
Q3 mentions how ties are handled
Excludes cancelled and pending orders and is aware that SUM ignores NULL amounts

rubric.label: Correct results
rubric.guide: 0 = queries would not give the asked result, 3 = two of three right or small logic slips, 5 = all three give the right result on the sample

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.guide: 0 = ignores status, NULLs and ties, 3 = handles some of them, 5 = handles cancelled/pending orders, NULL amounts, no-order customers and ties

rubric.label: Explanation
rubric.guide: 0 = no explanation, 3 = brief but partly unclear, 5 = short, clear notes on how each query works and why

rubric.label: Query quality
rubric.guide: 0 = hard to read or very inefficient, 3 = works but clumsy, 5 = readable, uses aliases and sensible date filters that can use indexes
